title: Corners and Yellow Cards per Match by League: One Match Table, SQL and pandas, 2025/26 vs 2026/27
summary:
Most football stat sites show you "corners per match" as a finished number. Computing it yourself takes about ten lines once all matches live in one table. Here is the exact approach we use for four leagues, with the real output for 2025/26 against 2026/27 so far. It is the same pipeline that produces our goal averages for every league, by TohaProBets, just pointed at corners and cards instead of goals.

The table

One row per match. Nothing is stored per team, because every team split can be derived later.

CREATE TABLE matches (
  league        TEXT,     -- 'APL', 'La Liga', 'Serie A', 'BR Serie A'
  season        TEXT,     -- '2526', '2627', or '2025', '2026' for Brazil
  date          TEXT,
  home, away    TEXT,
  hg, ag        INTEGER,  -- goals
  hc, ac        INTEGER,  -- corners won by each side
  hy, ay        INTEGER,  -- yellow cards
  referee       TEXT
);

A real row looks like this: ('2026-10-24', 'Arsenal', 'Everton', 2, 0, 12, 3, 1, 3, 'Tony Harrington'). Arsenal won 12 corners, Everton 3, and four yellows were shown.

Per-league averages in SQL 

SELECT league, season, COUNT(*) AS n,
       ROUND(AVG(hc + ac), 2) AS corners,
       ROUND(AVG(hy + ay), 2) AS yellows,
       ROUND(100.0 * AVG(hc + ac > 9.5), 1) AS corners_over_9_5,
       ROUND(100.0 * AVG(hy + ay > 4.5), 1) AS yellows_over_4_5
FROM matches
WHERE hc IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY league, season;

The WHERE hc IS NOT NULL line matters: friendlies and some cup games arrive without corner data, and averaging over NULLs silently shrinks the sample. In this dataset every league row has corners, so n equals the full match count.

The same in pandas 

df["corners"] = df.hc + df.ac
df["yellows"] = df.hy + df.ay
out = (df.dropna(subset=["hc"])
         .groupby(["league", "season"])
         .agg(n=("corners", "size"),
              corners=("corners", "mean"),
              yellows=("yellows", "mean"),
              c95=("corners", lambda s: (s > 9.5).mean() * 100),
              y45=("yellows", lambda s: (s > 4.5).mean() * 100))
         .round(2))

The output

European data runs to 8 November 2026, Brazil to 18 November.

League Season Matches Corners Over 9.5 Yellows Over 4.5
APL 2025/26 380 10.00 56.3% 3.75 33.9%
APL 2026/27 100 9.50 47.0% 4.01 39.0%
La Liga 2025/26 380 9.67 48.2% 4.41 44.2%
La Liga 2026/27 119 9.74 50.4% 4.44 48.7%
Serie A 2025/26 380 8.82 40.3% 3.70 30.8%
Serie A 2026/27 110 9.76 45.5% 3.22 26.4%
Brazil 2025 380 9.92 50.8% 4.93 56.3%
Brazil 2026 345 10.54 57.7% 4.58 49.0%

Three things jump out. England lost half a corner per match (10.00 to 9.50) but gained a quarter of a yellow (3.75 to 4.01). Serie A moved the other way on both: almost one extra corner (8.82 to 9.76) and half a card fewer (3.70 to 3.22). Brazil 2026 is the highest of all eight rows on both counts. The same aggregation for goals gives Serie A 3.11 per match against 2.43 last season.

Home and away splits

Split the sum back into its two columns and you get the home edge:

df.groupby(["league", "season"])[["hc", "ac", "hy", "ay"]].mean()

For 2026/27: APL home corners 5.00 against 4.50 away, La Liga 5.31 against 4.43, Serie A 5.03 against 4.74, Brazil 6.08 against 4.46. Away teams collect more yellows in England (2.23 against 1.78), while in Serie A the split is exactly level at 1.61 each.

Team level with one filter

The same table answers team questions. Newcastle's home corners this season:

SELECT AVG(hc), AVG(ac) FROM matches
WHERE league = 'APL' AND season = '2627' AND home = 'Newcastle';

Result: 3.6 won, 5.2 conceded over five games, down from 6.79 and 4.95 last season. A team-level number like this, set against the league baseline above, is the starting point for how Xpect turns match history into probabilities.

Pitfalls

  • Sample size. Ten rounds is 100 matches in England; a 0.5 shift is meaningful at league level but not for one team.
  • Season keys. Brazil runs on calendar years, Europe across two years. Keep the key as text and never sort it as an integer.
  • Corner direction. Store corners won by each side, not "for" and "against", and derive the latter per team. Otherwise the home and away views disagree.

title: `=?UTF-8?B?…?=` : lire et fabriquer des objets d'e-mail accentués sans casser les « é »
summary:
Vous avez déjà ouvert la source d'un e-mail (« Afficher l'original » dans Gmail, « Code source du message » dans Thunderbird) et vu une ligne comme celle-ci ?

Subject: =?UTF-8?B?UsOpdW5pb24gZCfDqXF1aXBlIDog?=
 =?UTF-8?B?Y29tcHRlIHJlbmR1IGR1IDE4IG5vdmVtYnJl?=

Ce n'est ni du chiffrement ni un bug : c'est un encoded-word au sens de la RFC 2047. Les en-têtes d'un e-mail ont été pensés pour de l'ASCII ; dès qu'un objet contient « é », « ç » ou « œ », il faut un moyen de faire passer ces octets dans un canal 7 bits. Base64 en est un. Voici comment ça marche, les trois pièges qui finissent en « R�union » dans les boîtes de réception, et comment vérifier un en-tête à la main.

Anatomie d'un encoded-word

Le format est toujours le même : =?charset?encodage?texte?=

  • charset : le jeu de caractères des octets, aujourd'hui presque toujours UTF-8 (on croise encore ISO-8859-1 ou windows-1252 dans de vieux messages) ;
  • encodage : B pour Base64, Q pour une variante de quoted-printable ;
  • texte : les octets encodés.

Le client mail décode le Base64, puis interprète les octets avec le charset annoncé. Si ce charset est faux, le décodage Base64 réussit quand même… et le texte affiché est faux. Base64 ne connaît pas les caractères : il ne transporte que des octets.

Exemple pas à pas (objet illustratif)

Prenons un objet fictif : Réunion d'équipe : compte rendu du 18 novembre.

  1. En octets UTF-8 : 46 caractères, mais 48 octets, car chaque « é » occupe deux octets (C3 A9). « Réunion » donne 52 C3 A9 75 6E 69 6F 6E.
  2. En Base64 : 48 octets donnent 64 caractères (48 ÷ 3 × 4, sans = final puisque 48 est divisible par 3) : UsOpdW5pb24gZCfDqXF1aXBlIDogY29tcHRlIHJlbmR1IGR1IDE4IG5vdmVtYnJl
  3. En encoded-word : =?UTF-8?B? + 64 caractères + ?=, soit 76 caractères.

Problème : la RFC 2047 limite un encoded-word à 75 caractères. Notre objet dépasse d'un seul caractère. C'est exactement le genre de cas qui passe en test avec « Réunion » tout court et casse en production avec un vrai objet.

La solution : découper le texte (pas la chaîne Base64), encoder chaque morceau séparément, puis placer les morceaux sur des lignes de continuation qui commencent par un espace :

  • Réunion d'équipe : (21 octets) → UsOpdW5pb24gZCfDqXF1aXBlIDog, encoded-word de 40 caractères ;
  • compte rendu du 18 novembre (27 octets) → Y29tcHRlIHJlbmR1IGR1IDE4IG5vdmVtYnJl, encoded-word de 48 caractères.

Le blanc de pliage entre deux encoded-words adjacents est ignoré à l'affichage ; l'espace visible fait partie du premier morceau. Vérification avec le parseur de la bibliothèque standard Python :

import email, email.policy

raw = (b"Subject: =?UTF-8?B?UsOpdW5pb24gZCfDqXF1aXBlIDog?=\r\n"
       b" =?UTF-8?B?Y29tcHRlIHJlbmR1IGR1IDE4IG5vdmVtYnJl?=\r\n\r\n")
msg = email.message_from_bytes(raw, policy=email.policy.default)
print(msg["Subject"])
# Réunion d'équipe : compte rendu du 18 novembre

Et l'étape 2 en JavaScript (Node) :

const b64 = Buffer.from("Réunion d'équipe : ", "utf8").toString("base64");
console.log(`=?UTF-8?B?${b64}?=`);
// =?UTF-8?B?UsOpdW5pb24gZCfDqXF1aXBlIDog?=

Piège n° 1 : couper au milieu d'un caractère

La tentation, c'est de découper la suite d'octets tous les N octets. Si on coupe après 12 octets, le premier morceau se termine par C3, le premier octet de « é », et le second commence par A9 :

  • UsOpdW5pb24gZCfD, décodé seul : Réunion d'�
  • qXF1aXBlIDog, décodé seul : �quipe :

La RFC 2047 est explicite : chaque encoded-word doit représenter un nombre entier de caractères ; un caractère multi-octet ne doit pas être réparti sur deux encoded-words. Certains décodeurs recollent les octets (le module email.header de Python le fait), d'autres affichent deux �. Ne comptez pas sur leur indulgence : coupez sur des frontières de caractères (en JavaScript, itérez avec for…of ou Array.from(str) plutôt qu'avec des index d'octets), et pensez aux emojis, qui prennent quatre octets.

Piège n° 2 : coller tout l'encoded-word dans un décodeur

Pour vérifier un en-tête, collez seulement la partie entre ?B? et ?=. Si vous collez =?UTF-8?B?…?= en entier dans un décodeur Base64 qui se contente d'écarter les caractères hors alphabet, il garde le = initial ainsi que les lettres et chiffres de UTF-8 et B. La chaîne obtenue n'est plus du Base64 valide : vous récoltez une erreur au lieu du texte.

Piège n° 3 : choisir « B » quand « Q » serait plus lisible

Pour un objet surtout ASCII, beaucoup de bibliothèques préfèrent l'encodage Q. Python (EmailMessage avec policy.SMTP) produit par exemple, pour le même objet :

Subject: =?utf-8?q?R=C3=A9union_d=27=C3=A9quipe?= : compte rendu du 18
 novembre

Seuls les mots qui en ont besoin sont encodés, et le reste reste lisible dans les logs. B est plus compact quand presque tout le texte est non-ASCII (arabe, japonais…). Les deux sont valides ; l'essentiel est de laisser votre bibliothèque mail générer l'en-tête plutôt que de concaténer des chaînes à la main.

Et le corps du message ?

Dans le corps, Base64 apparaît avec Content-Transfer-Encoding: base64, typiquement pour les pièces jointes. Là, c'est la RFC 2045 qui s'applique : lignes de 76 caractères au maximum. Quant aux noms de fichiers accentués des pièces jointes, ils passent souvent par une autre syntaxe (RFC 2231, filename*=UTF-8''… en encodage pourcent), qui n'est pas du Base64 du tout.

Vérifier un en-tête en 3 étapes avec l'outil

  1. Ouvrez le décodeur Base64 en français et laissez Jeu de Caractères sur UTF-8.
  2. Collez uniquement la charge utile, par exemple SMOpbMOobmUgRHVwcsOp (nom fictif). Conversion en Direct étant activée par défaut, le résultat s'affiche aussitôt : Hélène Dupré.
  3. Si l'outil signale des caractères de remplacement, le morceau a sans doute été coupé au milieu d'un caractère, ou le charset annoncé n'est pas UTF-8. Choisissez Hexadecimal (libellé en anglais) pour voir les octets bruts : C3 A9 correspond à « é » en UTF-8, un E9 isolé à « é » en Latin-1.

Pour l'opération inverse, l'encodeur Base64 fonctionne de la même façon. Il produit le Base64 brut : il n'ajoute ni =?UTF-8?B? ni ?= et ne découpe pas un objet trop long, c'est à vous (ou mieux, à votre bibliothèque) de le faire. Notez aussi que l'option « Couper les Lignes (64 chars) » coupe en réalité à 76 caractères, soit la limite du corps MIME, pas celle d'un encoded-word. La conversion se fait dans le navigateur, mais l'historique de l'outil garde les entrées courtes en stockage local : utilisez des exemples fictifs plutôt que de vrais en-têtes contenant des données personnelles.

Transparence : cet outil est proposé par Mind vs Drive, l'équipe derrière ce blog.

À retenir

  • =?UTF-8?B?…?=, c'est un charset plus du Base64 ; ce n'est pas du chiffrement.
  • 75 caractères au maximum par encoded-word : découpez le texte, pas le Base64, et jamais au milieu d'un caractère multi-octet.
  • Pour déboguer, décodez seulement la charge utile et regardez les octets en hexadécimal.

Références : RFC 2047 (encoded-words, limite de 75 caractères, caractères non découpables), RFC 2045 (Content-Transfer-Encoding, lignes de 76 caractères), RFC 2231 (paramètres comme filename*). Exemples vérifiés le 19 novembre 2026.

title: What Happens When We Define the Same Function Multiple Times? In Python
summary:
What Happens When We Define the Same Function Multiple Times?

In Python, if we define the same function name more than once, the latest function definition replaces the previous definition.

When we call that function, Python executes the latest definition.

Example: 

def greet():
    print("Hello")

def greet():
    print("Welcome to Python")

greet()

Output:

Welcome to Python

Explanation:

  1. First, we define the greet() function, which prints "Hello".
  2. Next, we define another function with the same name greet().
  3. The second definition replaces the first one.
  4. When we call greet(), Python executes the second function.

title: Measuring 37,426 Generated Answers to Find Out What the Prompt Actually Controls
summary:
Our flashcard generator produces answers that all come out around sixty words. I assumed the prompt had a word target. It doesn't — it has a sentence target, and the word count is downstream of how dense the source book happens to be.

Here's how that got measured, and why the first explanation I wrote down was wrong.

The data is already in the HTML

Every deck page ships its whole deck inline:

window.BC_CARDS = [{ "id": "a--01", "ch": "c01", "q": "...", "a": "...", "ref": "Chapter 1" }, ...];

So there's no API to write, no headless browser, no pagination. Fetch 217 sitemap URLs, keep the 174 that are decks, pull the array with a regex, json.loads it. 67 seconds on four threads. 37,426 cards.

One deck broke the parser: Unterminated string starting at char 95,083. A quote escaping bug in our own build, not in the content. It costs one deck out of 174 and it's on the list.

The distribution

Words Cards Share
<30 15 0.04%
30–39 268 0.7%
40–49 2,611 7.0%
50–59 13,027 34.8%
60–69 16,261 43.4%
70–79 4,687 12.5%
80–89 499 1.3%
90–99 48 0.13%
100+ 10 0.03%

Mean 60.93, σ 8.25, median 61, min 25, max 109.

Three results

No truncation anywhere. Zero of 37,426 answers end without terminal punctuation. And there's no pile-up at a ceiling — the max of 109 occurs exactly once, 58 cards clear 90 words, 10 clear 100, none clear 120. A length clamp produces a spike at the clamp value plus a pile of unfinished sentences. Neither is present.

Sentence count is what's pinned, not word count. 86.7% of the library is two or three sentences (14,722 and 17,731 respectively). Answer length is then sentences × words per sentence, and the second term is the one with range in it.

Deck Cards Words Sentences Words/sentence
Meditations 25 40.88 2.68 16.19
The Art of War 24 43.29 2.79 16.27
The Prince 32 46.41 2.62 18.49
Tao Te Ching 270 50.12 2.51 21.05
Discourses on Livy 531 59.09 2.51 25.06

Site average is 24.50 words per sentence. The five shortest decks are the five aphoristic classics, in the exact order of their sentence density. Not one narrative history among them.

Nothing else predicts it. Correlation between deck card count and mean answer length: 0.04 over 174 decks. Between question length and answer length: 0.05. Chapter structure is unchanged from the previous run — 7,963 of 10,050 chapters hold exactly four cards (79.2%), and only 4 answer pairs out of 37,426 share their first 120 characters.

The bit I can't measure

The payload has no chapter text. I can't tell whether Meditations produces 16-word sentences because Marcus Aurelius wrote short lines or because that deck was generated with a different setting. Identical output either way. I also didn't validate any answer against its book.

Retraction

Six days ago I wrote that the answers "sit in a 60-word band, which suggests a 60-word target." Wrong cause, right arithmetic. If the prompt constrains anything, it's the sentence count; the word band is a side effect of the source's own density. Which means the useful knob for making answers longer is not "add a sentence." It's picking a book that writes longer ones.

Disclosure: WakeCards is ours. Everything above came from crawling our own pages on 19 November 2026 — 37,426 cards, all public, all reproducible with curl and forty lines of Python.

If you've generated Q&A pairs from text before: does your output length track the source, or the prompt? I've stopped trusting my own guess about which.

title: Deploy a LangGraph agent to a public URL
summary:
You have a LangGraph graph that works in a notebook. Now someone else needs to call it: a teammate, a Telegram bot, a CRM that posts a question and waits for an answer. That means a web API, a server that stays up, pinned dependencies, a secret for your model key, and a URL that not everyone on the internet can spend your model budget through.

This walkthrough takes a small LangGraph agent from a folder on your laptop to a public HTTPS address on uagents8, then locks that address with a token. In our run on 28 October 2026 the agent was live 78 seconds after we created it; the build took about 38 of them.

What we're deploying

One graph, two nodes, one branch:

START --(the question is arithmetic)--> calculate --> END
START --(anything else)--------------> respond   --> END

calculate is a tool node in plain Python. respond is where your model goes; until you add one, it answers with a labelled stub, so the whole thing runs with no key and no network. The graph sits behind FastAPI with one route that matters, POST /ask.

import ast
import operator
import os
from typing import TypedDict

import uvicorn
from fastapi import FastAPI
from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field


class State(TypedDict):
    question: str
    answer: str
    mode: str  # "tool", "stub" or "model"


_OPERATORS = {ast.Add: operator.add, ast.Sub: operator.sub, ast.Mult: operator.mul, ast.Div: operator.truediv}


def _evaluate(node: ast.AST) -> float:
    """Evaluate + - * / and parentheses on numbers; anything else raises ValueError."""
    if isinstance(node, ast.Expression):
        return _evaluate(node.body)
    if isinstance(node, ast.Constant) and isinstance(node.value, (int, float)):
        return node.value
    if isinstance(node, ast.UnaryOp) and isinstance(node.op, ast.USub):
        return -_evaluate(node.operand)
    if isinstance(node, ast.BinOp) and type(node.op) in _OPERATORS:
        return _OPERATORS[type(node.op)](_evaluate(node.left), _evaluate(node.right))
    raise ValueError("unsupported expression")


def _arithmetic(question: str) -> str | None:
    """The expression inside `question`, if the whole question is just arithmetic."""
    expression = question.strip().lower().removeprefix("what is").strip().rstrip("?= ")
    if not expression or not any(ch.isdigit() for ch in expression):
        return None
    if any(ch not in "0123456789+-*/(). " for ch in expression):
        return None
    return expression


def route(state: State) -> str:
    return "calculate" if _arithmetic(state["question"]) else "respond"


def calculate(state: State) -> dict:
    expression = _arithmetic(state["question"]) or ""
    try:
        result = _evaluate(ast.parse(expression, mode="eval"))
    except (SyntaxError, ValueError, ArithmeticError):
        return {"answer": f"I could not calculate {expression!r}.", "mode": "tool"}
    return {"answer": f"{expression} = {result:g}", "mode": "tool"}


def respond(state: State) -> dict:
    # Your model call goes here. The key comes from the environment, never from this file.
    return {"answer": f"[stub] You asked: {state['question']}", "mode": "stub"}


builder = StateGraph(State)
builder.add_node("calculate", calculate)
builder.add_node("respond", respond)
builder.add_conditional_edges(START, route, {"calculate": "calculate", "respond": "respond"})
builder.add_edge("calculate", END)
builder.add_edge("respond", END)
graph = builder.compile()

app = FastAPI()


class Ask(BaseModel):
    question: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=500)


@app.post("/ask")
def ask(body: Ask) -> dict:
    result = graph.invoke({"question": body.question, "answer": "", "mode": ""})
    return {"question": body.question, "answer": result["answer"], "mode": result["mode"]}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    uvicorn.run(app, host="0.0.0.0", port=int(os.environ.get("PORT", "8000")))

_arithmetic and _evaluate accept + - * / and parentheses on numbers and nothing else, so user input never reaches eval. A malformed expression gets a polite answer, not a crash.

Three things the platform needs from your code

1. Listen on PORT, on 0.0.0.0. The last two lines do it. The platform sets PORT; a server bound to 127.0.0.1 runs fine and can never be reached.

2. Start listening before anything slow. The health check only asks whether the port accepts connections. It requests no route, so an API with only /ask is fine. It gives the port about 150 seconds to open. Load big models or indexes after the server is up, or lazily on the first request.

3. Pin every dependency. The build runs Python 3.12 with no compiler, so pick versions that ship wheels. In a clean virtual environment:

pip install fastapi uvicorn langgraph
pip freeze > requirements.txt

The sample pins fastapi==0.143.3, uvicorn==0.54.0 and langgraph==1.2.16. main.py and requirements.txt sit at the top level, and the platform runs python main.py. There is no build file to write: the platform works out the build from your code, and if your project already has its own build file at the top level, it uses that as written.

Deploy it

Push the folder to a GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket repository, or zip main.py and requirements.txt.

In the dashboard, press + Deploy Agent:

  1. Source: pick your Git provider and the repository. Every push to the branch redeploys. Or pick Code Archive and upload the zip.
  2. Configure: keep Continuous Service and choose a Resource size. Sizes are memory limits: T is 256 MB, S 512 MB, L 1 GB. In our run this agent used about 80 MB, so T is enough.
  3. Confirm, then Deploy agent.

The status screen moves from Building agent to Starting your agent to Running. Ours took 78 seconds, uploaded as a zip, with no model key. The agent's page then shows its public URL.

Call it 

curl -X POST https://<your-agent-url>/ask \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"question": "what is 2+3*4?"}'

Ask it anything else and you get the stub, with "mode": "stub". That's your sign that the branch to the model is wired and waiting.

Put your provider's client library in requirements.txt (pinned) and replace the body of respond() with the call. The key never goes into the code or the repository.

Open the agent's Settings tab, find Access tokens and choose Generate agent token. Give it a name you'll recognise (crm, telegram-bot) and pick how long it stays valid: 7, 30 or 90 days, or no expiry. Copy it. It starts with uagt_live_ and is shown only once.

It will, sooner or later: a package you installed locally and never pinned, a variable you renamed in one file and not the other, a server bound to localhost. The failed agent's page explains the error in plain language. If you press Fix with AI, it reads the error and your code, patches a copy, checks the patch before building it, and deploys the fixed copy as a new version. title: Functions in Python
summary:
1. What is a Function in Python?

  • A function is a block of reusable code that performs a specific task. Instead of writing the same code repeatedly, we can define a function once and call it whenever needed.

  • Functions help to reduce code repetition, improve code readability, and make programs easier to maintain.

  • Python provides the def keyword to define a function.

Syntax: 

def function_name():
    # function body
    statements

Example: 

def greet():
    print("Hello, Welcome to Python")

greet()

Output:

Hello, Welcome to Python

Explanation:

  • def is the keyword used to define a function.
  • greet is the function name.
  • The statements inside the function form the function body.
  • greet() is the function call used to execute the function.

2. Why Do We Use Functions?

Functions provide several advantages:

  1. Code Reusability – Write code once and use it multiple times.
  2. Code Readability – Makes the program easier to understand.
  3. Code Organization – Divides a large program into smaller parts.
  4. Easy Maintenance – Changes can be made in one place.
  5. Avoid Code Repetition – Reduces duplicate code.

3. Types of Functions in Python

Python functions can be classified into two main types:

  1. Built-in Functions
  2. User-defined Functions

1. Built-in Functions

Built-in functions are predefined functions provided by Python. We can use them directly without defining them.

Some commonly used built-in functions are:

Function Description
print() Displays output
input() Gets input from the user
len() Returns the length
type() Returns the data type

Example:

numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40]

print(len(numbers))

Output:

4

2. User-defined Functions

User-defined functions are functions created by programmers to perform specific tasks.

The def keyword is used to create user-defined functions.

Example:

def add():
    a = 10
    b = 20
    print(a + b)

add()

Output:

30

4. Types of User-defined Functions Based on Arguments and Return Values

Based on arguments and return values, functions can be divided into four types.

1. Function Without Arguments and Without Return Value

This function does not accept any arguments and does not return any value.

Example:

def display():
    print("Welcome to Python")

display()

Output:

Welcome to Python

2. Function With Arguments and Without Return Value

This function accepts arguments but does not return any value.

Example:

def add(a, b):
    print(a + b)

add(10, 20)

Output:

30

Here, a and b receive the values passed during the function call.

3. Function Without Arguments and With Return Value

This function does not accept arguments but returns a value using the return keyword.

Example:

def add():
    a = 10
    b = 20
    return a + b

result = add()
print(result)

Output:

30

Here, the function calculates the result and sends it back to the caller using return.

4. Function With Arguments and With Return Value

This function accepts arguments and returns a result.

Example:

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(10, 20)
print(result)

Output:

30

This is one of the most commonly used function types in Python.

Conclusion

Functions are an important concept in Python programming. They help developers write reusable, organized, and maintainable code.

Understanding function definitions, arguments, parameters, return statements provides a strong foundation for developing Python applications.

1. What is a Function in Python?

  • A function is a block of reusable code that performs a specific task. Instead of writing the same code repeatedly, we can define a function once and call it whenever needed.

  • Functions help to reduce code repetition, improve code readability, and make programs easier to maintain.

  • Python provides the def keyword to define a function.

Syntax: 

def function_name():
    # function body
    statements

Example: 

def greet():
    print("Hello, Welcome to Python")

greet()

Output:

Hello, Welcome to Python

Explanation:

  • def is the keyword used to define a function.
  • greet is the function name.
  • The statements inside the function form the function body.
  • greet() is the function call used to execute the function.

2. Why Do We Use Functions?

Functions provide several advantages:

  1. Code Reusability – Write code once and use it multiple times.
  2. Code Readability – Makes the program easier to understand.
  3. Code Organization – Divides a large program into smaller parts.
  4. Easy Maintenance – Changes can be made in one place.
  5. Avoid Code Repetition – Reduces duplicate code.

3. Types of Functions in Python

Python functions can be classified into two main types:

  1. Built-in Functions
  2. User-defined Functions

1. Built-in Functions

Built-in functions are predefined functions provided by Python. We can use them directly without defining them.

Some commonly used built-in functions are:

Function Description
print() Displays output
input() Gets input from the user
len() Returns the length
type() Returns the data type

Example:

numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40]

print(len(numbers))

Output:

4

2. User-defined Functions

User-defined functions are functions created by programmers to perform specific tasks.

The def keyword is used to create user-defined functions.

Example:

def add():
    a = 10
    b = 20
    print(a + b)

add()

Output:

30

4. Types of User-defined Functions Based on Arguments and Return Values

Based on arguments and return values, functions can be divided into four types.

1. Function Without Arguments and Without Return Value

This function does not accept any arguments and does not return any value.

Example:

def display():
    print("Welcome to Python")

display()

Output:

Welcome to Python

2. Function With Arguments and Without Return Value

This function accepts arguments but does not return any value.

Example:

def add(a, b):
    print(a + b)

add(10, 20)

Output:

30

Here, a and b receive the values passed during the function call.

3. Function Without Arguments and With Return Value

This function does not accept arguments but returns a value using the return keyword.

Example:

def add():
    a = 10
    b = 20
    return a + b

result = add()
print(result)

Output:

30

Here, the function calculates the result and sends it back to the caller using return.

4. Function With Arguments and With Return Value

This function accepts arguments and returns a result.

Example:

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

result = add(10, 20)
print(result)

Output:

30

This is one of the most commonly used function types in Python.

Conclusion

Functions are an important concept in Python programming. They help developers write reusable, organized, and maintainable code.

Understanding function definitions, arguments, parameters, return statements provides a strong foundation for developing Python applications.

title: How to tell whether a physics simulation blew up during RL training
summary:
When you train a policy across thousands of parallel simulated worlds, a few of them will explode: a body starts inside the floor, an energy spike throws parts across the scene, a value turns into NaN. If those worlds keep feeding observations and rewards, the policy learns from garbage and you find out hours later. This walkthrough shows how to catch them with Alloy, an open-source physics engine for robot learning that grades every world as it runs.

pip install alloy-engine

1. Three worlds, one of them broken on purpose 

import numpy as np
import alloy

z = np.array([0.3, 0.0, 0.6])        # world 1 starts with its cube half inside the ground
pos = np.stack([np.zeros(3), np.zeros(3), z], axis=1)
scene = alloy.Scene(worlds=3, dt=0.01)
scene.add_ground()
scene.add_box("block", size=(0.1, 0.1, 0.1), pos=pos, mass=0.2)
sim = alloy.build(scene, device="cpu")
sim.run(0.8)
for w, row in enumerate(sim.health()["worlds"]):
    flags = [f for f in row["flags"] if f != "DET_DOWNGRADED"]
    print(w, row["severity"], flags)

0 OK []
1 INVALID ['PEN_WARN', 'PEN_FAIL', 'ENERGY_JUMP', 'LATCHED', 'START_PEN']
2 OK []

Every world gets a grade: OK, DEGRADED or INVALID. World 1 started with its cube overlapping the ground, so it was flagged for penetration and an energy jump, then frozen at its last good state while the other two worlds carried on.

2. Trust the check, not the picture 

check = sim.check()
print(check["ok"])
print(sim.state(["block"])["block.pos"][:, 2].round(2))
for p in check["problems"]:
    print(p["world"], p["level"], p["check"])

False
[0.05 0.   0.05]
1 fail start_overlap
1 error health
1 error penetration
0 warn health
2 warn health

The frozen world sits calmly at z = 0, which looks fine in a render. check()["ok"] is the value to trust, and each problem names its world and the check that failed. The warn rows for worlds 0 and 2 record a flag that fired during the landing and cleared; those worlds stay OK.

3. In a training environment it is automatic

With Alloy's Gymnasium-style vector environments you do not reset anything by hand. A frozen world ends its episode, returns zero reward and observation, and starts again, and the environment counts it:

import numpy as np
import alloy.envs

env = alloy.envs.make("GripperLift-v0", num_envs=4)
obs, info = env.reset(seed=0)
for _ in range(20):
    obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info = env.step(env.xp.asarray(np.zeros((4, 3), np.float32)))
print(np.asarray(info["invalid"]).tolist(), np.asarray(env.invalid_episodes).tolist())

info["invalid"] marks the worlds frozen on this step and env.invalid_episodes counts frozen episodes per world. Log that count during training: a rising number means the task or the physics settings need attention.

Keep in mind

  • The health check does not catch every overlap between rigid bodies and robot parts, and a fast body can pass through a thin static part before any flag fires.
  • A GPU run does not repeat bit for bit once bodies touch in more than one place.
  • The docs keep the full list of limits.

Links

  • Docs page this is based on: https://alloy.argonrobotics.ai/docs/answers/did-my-simulation-blow-up/
  • Code: https://github.com/argonrobotics-ai/alloy
  • Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.16312

title: I built a 37-line static site generator. Then I ran it on real markdown.
summary:
I have a small pile of side projects, and one of them is staticgen: a static site generator in Python with no dependencies at all. The goal was not to replace Hugo. The goal was to understand it.

The first version is 37 lines. It reads a folder of markdown, turns it into HTML, and drops it into a template:

def render(post_md, template):
    lines = post_md.strip().split("\n")
    out = []
    for line in lines:
        if line.startswith("# "):
            out.append("
" + line[2:] + "
")
        elif line.startswith("## "):
            out.append("
" + line[3:] + "
")
        else:
            line = line.replace("**", "", 1).replace("**", "", 1)
            out.append("
" + line + "
")
    body = "\n".join(out)
    title = lines[0].lstrip("# ").strip()
    return template.replace(TITLE, title).replace(BODY, body)

It worked on the one test post I wrote. Then I fed it something realistic, and it fell apart in four ways worth knowing about.

1. The bold replacement eats exactly one pair

That .replace("**", ..., 1) chain is a neat trick that breaks the moment a line has two bold runs. Actual output from the code above, on Some **bold** and **more bold** here.:

Some bold and **more bold** here.

The first ** became , the second became , and the remaining four asterisks were left alone. Any line with more than one bold span renders literally.

The fix is not a better loop over replace. It is one regex pass that consumes both cases:

BOLD = re.compile(r"\*\*(.+?)\*\*")
line = BOLD.sub(r"\1", line)

.+? is lazy, so it matches the shortest run between two delimiters. That handles one pair or ten, and it fails visibly instead of silently leaving artifacts.

2. Nothing is escaped

This line went straight through:

a < b && c > d

A naked < makes browsers guess, and the guess is not always what you want. Escape first, then add markup:

import html
line = html.escape(line, quote=False)

Do it before the bold pass, otherwise you escape your own tags. Order matters here, and it stays hidden until a post mentions generics or a comparison operator.

3. Every blank line becomes an empty paragraph 



Some bold here.

Harmless-looking, annoying in practice: it adds gaps you cannot style away without an :empty rule, and it bloats the HTML of ordinary prose. Skip blank lines and let them separate paragraphs instead:

if not line.strip():
    continue

4. Fenced code blocks get mangled, which is the real bug

A fenced block came out as three paragraphs, and markdown inside the code was interpreted. The fence markers ended up wrapped in

tags, and **not bold** was bolded inside what should have been literal code.

For a developer blog this is fatal. Code samples are the content. A line-by-line renderer with no state cannot handle it, so the renderer needs a mode switch:

in_code = False
for line in lines:
    if line.startswith("```"):
        out.append("
" if not in_code else "
")
        in_code = not in_code
        continue
    if in_code:
        out.append(html.escape(line))
        continue
    ...

That is the whole lesson of the project, and it is the same lesson every time I have written a small parser: the naive version is not wrong about the concept, it is wrong about state. Bold spans, fences, lists, and escaping all need to know what came before.

Where it stands

staticgen is now about 90 lines, still dependency-free, and it builds my posts without surprises. It has a --template flag and a sample post in posts/. It is not a Hugo competitor: no incremental builds, no taxonomies, no front matter beyond a leading # heading.

What it gave me was cheap. Two hours, and now I know exactly why the markdown pipeline in every tool I use is more complicated than it looks.

If you want the same exercise, pick the smallest tool you rely on and rewrite the dumb version of it. The bugs will teach you more than the docs.

title: Run Mobilerun with local and cheap models Ollama, DeepSeek, Qwen, OpenRouter
summary:
Every step a phone agent takes is a model call. Read the screen, pick one action, tap, repeat. A simple task can be 10 of those. A test suite can be thousands.

So the first question people ask after getting Mobilerun working is always the same: can I run this on something cheaper? Or on my own machine, with no API key at all?

Yes. The open-source Mobilerun framework doesn't care where the model lives. This post shows what runs where, the exact local setup with Ollama and Qwen, the hosted setup for DeepSeek and OpenRouter, and what actually changes your results.

The problem with "which model is best?"

You'll find plenty of opinions about which model is best for phone agents. You won't find a published Mobilerun benchmark broken out by Ollama, DeepSeek, Qwen and OpenRouter. We haven't published one yet either.

That matters, because the answer depends on things only you know: your tasks, your device, your hardware, and whether you run with vision. So instead of a ranking, we'll give you the setup for each option and a simple way to measure them on your own work.

What runs where

The Mobilerun framework runs on your machine. It controls an Android device through Portal and ADB. The LLM provider is a separate choice you make in config or on the command line.

Here's how the options split:

  • Ollama runs inference locally. No model API key.
  • DeepSeek is a hosted API. It uses DEEPSEEK_API_KEY.
  • OpenRouter is a hosted API that routes to many models. It uses OPENROUTER_API_KEY.
  • Qwen is a model family, not a provider. You can run Qwen locally through Ollama, and Qwen models are also available through hosted providers like OpenRouter.

Install and run it locally with Ollama and Qwen

You need Python 3.11 to 3.13. Python 3.14 isn't supported yet, and the docs warn that installing on 3.14 silently falls back to an old version. You also need ADB and an Android device with USB debugging on.

Install the framework:

Install Ollama, connect your Android device, then set up Portal and check the connection.

mobilerun setupmobilerun pingCopy

If ping prints "Portal is installed and accessible. You're good to go!", you're ready. Pull the model and run a task:

ollama pull qwen3:8bmobilerun run "Turn on dark mode" --provider Ollama --model qwen3:8b --base_url http://localhost:11434Copy

That's the whole loop running on your hardware. The framework talks to Ollama at localhost:11434, and no request leaves your machine for inference.

Pass --provider and --model together. The CLI guide is clear that passing only one makes the run fail before the agent starts.

To make Ollama the default instead of typing flags every time, add a profile to your config file. Mobilerun creates it at ~/.config/droidrun/config.yaml on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/droidrun/config.yaml on macOS, and %LOCALAPPDATA%\droidrun\droidrun\config.yaml on Windows. Yes, the folder still says droidrun. You can also point MOBILERUN_CONFIG or --config at your own file.

One Ollama detail worth knowing: Mobilerun sets the context size itself. The default context_window is 32,768, which keeps most models on the GPU. Setting it to -1 asks for the model's full context, which preallocates the whole KV cache and can spill onto your CPU.

DeepSeek and OpenRouter: hosted, pay per call

For the hosted options, set the key and pick the provider and model with CLI flags.

DeepSeek:

export DEEPSEEK_API_KEY=your-keymobilerun run "Turn on dark mode" --provider DeepSeek --model deepseek-flashCopy

OpenRouter, here with a hosted Qwen model:

export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=your-keymobilerun run "Turn on dark mode" --provider OpenRouter --model qwen/qwen3.8-flashCopy

Or save them as profiles so every run uses them:

llm_profiles:  fast_agent:    provider: DeepSeek    model: deepseek-flashllm_profiles:  fast_agent:    provider: OpenRouter    model: qwen/qwen3.8-flashCopy

A note on mobilerun configure. The wizard's provider list today is gemini, openai, anthropic, xai, ollama, openai_like, minimax and zai. DeepSeek and OpenRouter aren't in it as named options, so use the CLI flags or the YAML profile for those. Model IDs change often on both services, so check DeepSeek's and OpenRouter's model lists before you copy ours.

What affects your results

Swapping the model is one line. Whether the task finishes is a different story. These are the four things that change the outcome.

Accessibility tree by default. Out of the box, the agent reads Android's accessibility tree, a structured list of what's on screen with text and bounds. No screenshots. That works with text-only models, including qwen3:8b.

--vision adds screenshots. With vision on, the agent gets a screenshot alongside the tree on every step. That needs a vision-capable model. If you test vision on a local model, pull one that accepts images. For local vision models that downsize images in a way Mobilerun can't detect, the docs suggest capping the screenshot so tap coordinates stay accurate:

agent:  model_screenshot_max_side: 1280Copy

There's also --vision-only, which drops the tree and drives the device from screenshots alone.

Native tool calling vs the fallback protocol. Mobilerun uses native tool calling where the model supports it. title: Pointing the OpenAI Python and Node SDKs at a model with fewer refusals
summary:
Disclosure: I work on InterOdin, the API used in this tutorial. The pattern works for any OpenAI-compatible provider.

Security scripts often hit a wall with general-purpose models: a request to explain a malware sample from your own incident, or to draft a detection rule, comes back as a refusal. If your code already uses the official OpenAI SDK, you can switch the model behind it with a base URL and a key. This walkthrough uses Odin v1 through InterOdin, which serves both Chat Completions and Responses.

Install 

pip install openai     # Python
npm install openai     # JavaScript / TypeScript

Configure the client

Python:

import os

from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url="https://api.interodin.com/v1",
    api_key=os.environ["INTERODIN_API_KEY"],
)

completion = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="odin-v1",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hello in Romanian."}],
)
print(completion.choices[0].message.content)

TypeScript:

import OpenAI from 'openai'

const client = new OpenAI({
  baseURL: 'https://api.interodin.com/v1',
  apiKey: process.env.INTERODIN_API_KEY,
})

const completion = await client.chat.completions.create({
  model: 'odin-v1',
  messages: [{ role: 'user', content: 'Say hello in Romanian.' }],
})
console.log(completion.choices[0]?.message.content)

No code changes at all? Both SDKs read these environment variables:

export OPENAI_BASE_URL="https://api.interodin.com/v1"
export OPENAI_API_KEY="io-sk-your-key"

Responses API 

response = client.responses.create(model="odin-v1", input="Say hello in Romanian.", store=False)
print(response.output_text)

Responses is stateless here: send the full conversation in input on each turn.

What doesn't carry over

  • Images and files. Odin v1 is text-only. Images are replaced by a text note; a file in the newest message fails with 400 unsupported_content.
  • Hosted tools (file search, code interpreter, MCP) are removed from the request. Your own function tools run. Web search works on the Responses API only, billed per search.
  • previous_response_id, conversation and background: true return 400 unsupported_parameter, and stored responses can't be fetched, because nothing is stored.

Errors

The SDKs raise their usual exceptions: AuthenticationError for 401, RateLimitError for 429, and APIStatusError / APIError subclasses for the rest. Read the code field to tell insufficient_credits (402) apart from other errors. 429 and 5xx are retried automatically.

Billing is prepaid credits per token, with no subscription, and API prompts and completions are not stored. Fewer refusals does not mean no rules: the Acceptable Use Policy forbids illegal and harmful uses, so use it on systems and data you are authorised to work on.

The maintained version of this guide lives in the docs: https://docs.interodin.com/en/integrations/openai-sdk
